Volume 06 · Chapter 10

Trade and comparative advantage

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v06-c09

By the endDerive gains and distributional effects from trade models.

Volume 6 · Chapter 10

Trade changes what an economy can consume, what its factors earn and which firms can serve a market. A gain in feasible national consumption does not identify who receives that gain. Derive the production choices, clear the markets and keep the transfers in the welfare ledger.

Capability: derive gains and distributional effects in explicit trade models, solve an export-selection decision and reconcile tariff welfare under alternative foreign supply responses. Prerequisites: fiscal resources and distribution, production and costs, competitive surplus, general equilibrium and market power.

What exactly is gained, and by whom?

A country can import a good that its workers could produce themselves. This is worthwhile when exporting something else buys more of the import than the same resources could produce at home. The comparison uses opportunity costs, not wages alone. A low wage can reflect low productivity; a high wage can coexist with low unit cost. Nor does an export surplus by itself measure a benefit: exports use resources and imports deliver goods. Here the first models have balanced trade in one period; later chapters allow borrowing, asset transactions and income from abroad.

All numbers below are original synthetic examples, not observations about any country or current tariff system. Quantities are units produced or consumed during one common period. Labor is hours supplied in that period; capital in the factor model is a flow of machine services, not a security or a debt stock. Goods and factors are divisible. An endowment is fixed during each comparison. No adjustment unemployment, pollution, transport cost or policy cost is silently included: when a model introduces one, its equations change explicitly.

A terms-of-trade ratio is the price of a country's export good divided by the price of its import good. A rise buys more imports per export unit, holding other conditions fixed. It is a goods-price ratio. It differs from the home-currency-per-foreign-currency exchange quote introduced in Chapter 11. Normalize the price of a specified good or transferable numeraire to one; this changes units, not real resources.

Ricardian technology: compare the costs of giving something up

There are two countries, Home and Foreign, and two goods, cloth C and wheat W. In country i, aCi and aWi are strictly positive labor hours needed per unit. Labor Li > 0 moves freely between domestic sectors, but not internationally. Constant returns, competitive firms, identical labor within a country and costless goods trade are maintained. Feasible production satisfies

aCiQCi + aWiQWi ≤ Li,   QCi,QWi ≥ 0.

One more unit of cloth uses labor that could make aCi/aWi units of wheat. Thus Home has comparative advantage in cloth if aCH/aWH < aCF/aWF. Absolute advantage means needing fewer hours for a particular good. A country can have absolute advantage in both goods while having comparative advantage in only one. Multiplying both of a country's labor requirements by the same positive number changes productivity levels but not that country's opportunity-cost ratio.

Set PW = 1 and p = PC/PW > 0. Revenue per labor hour is p/aCi in cloth and 1/aWi in wheat. Maximizing pQCi + QWi over the triangular production set therefore gives a global choice: all cloth if p exceeds aCi/aWi, all wheat if it is below, and every full-employment combination on the frontier at equality. This follows from a linear objective: moving one hour toward the higher-valued use raises revenue until the boundary. At equality the production choice is a correspondence, not a unique point. The competitive wage equals the larger revenue per hour; the unused sector cannot afford that wage at its output price.

To close demand, let all households have u(C,W) = √(CW), with positive income, no saving and ownership of domestic labor. Their budget is pC + W ≤ m. Substituting W = m−pC makes utility squared C(m−pC), a strictly concave quadratic, so C = m/(2p), W = m/2 is the unique optimum. In autarky, with both goods demanded, p equals domestic opportunity cost and consumption equals production. Under trade, prices must also clear both world goods markets; an arbitrary price between opportunity costs describes feasible specialization incentives, not automatically equilibrium.

Worked example 1 — Clear both markets and the international payment

One-period technologies and labor
CountryHours per clothHours per wheatLabor hoursCloth opportunity cost
Home241201/2 wheat
Foreign631202 wheat

Autarky allocates half the labor expenditure to each good. Home produces and consumes (C,W) = (30,15); Foreign (10,20). Consider complete specialization at 1/2 < p < 2. Home produces 60 cloth and earns 60p; Foreign produces 40 wheat and earns 40. Total cloth demand is (60p+40)/(2p) = 30+20/p. Equating it to 60 gives p = 2/3, inside the proposed interval. Wheat demand is (60p+40)/2 = 40, equal to supply. This verifies the candidate branch.

Both national incomes are 40 wheat units and each country consumes (30,20). Home exports 30 cloth, worth (2/3)30 = 20 wheat, and imports 20 wheat. Foreign has the opposite transactions. No foreign gift, borrowing or unrecorded payment finances the extra consumption. Home's consumption would require 2(30)+4(20) = 140 domestic hours, above its 120; Foreign's would require 240. Trade expands consumption possibilities without changing either technology.

Utility squared rises from 450 to 600 at Home and from 200 to 600 abroad. Home's wheat wage rises from 1/4 to 1/3, while its cloth wage stays 1/2; Foreign's wheat wage stays 1/3 and its cloth wage rises from 1/6 to 1/2. These are gains for the homogeneous labor owners in this particular model. They do not prove that workers facing costly retraining or owners of another factor gain in a different economy.

A precise feasible-gains argument and its boundary

Let QA be an autarky production/consumption bundle and QT maximize production value at positive trade prices P. Since QA remains technologically feasible, P·QT ≥ P·QA. A representative consumer receiving all that production income can therefore still afford the old bundle; utility maximization delivers weakly higher utility. The argument requires the old technology to remain available, correct ownership income and a feasible trade budget. Strict improvement needs more: equality prices, tastes or a zero-trade equilibrium can leave utility unchanged. It is not a proof that everyone can afford their old bundle under the new distribution of income.

For the two-country Ricardian model, a positive-demand equilibrium price cannot lie strictly below both opportunity costs or above both: world production would omit a demanded good. At either endpoint one country can diversify. If opportunity costs coincide, specialization does not create this source of gains. Transport costs can consume gains; policy distortions or externalities invalidate the simple efficient-production comparison unless incorporated. Real adjustment costs require a dated transition, not a claim that their effects vanish because this static benchmark omits them.

The method reference is Costinot's MIT 14.54 Ricardian lecture, especially its unit-labor technology, specialization and wage conditions. The equilibrium numbers, feasibility checks and boundary problem here are original.

Factor endowments can create trade and persistent distributive losses

Now replace the one-factor technology with two goods X,Y and two domestic factors L,K. A unit of X requires exactly two labor hours and one machine-service unit; a unit of Y requires one labor hour and two machine-service units. These fixed coefficients allow no substitution within a technique. Both factors move between domestic sectors, cannot move abroad and are competitively rented. Both countries have the same technology and the same √(XY) preferences. Normalize PY = 1 and write p = PX/PY. Here w and r are respectively Y units per labor hour and per machine-service unit; r is a rental price, not an interest rate.

With both goods produced and both factors fully used, solve the resource and zero-profit equations:

2X + Y = L,   X + 2Y = K   ⇒   X = (2L−K)/3,   Y = (2K−L)/3.
2w + r = p,   w + 2r = 1   ⇒   w = (2p−1)/3,   r = (2−p)/3.

The strict diversification cone is K/2 < L < 2K, with K > 0: it makes X,Y positive. Positive factor rewards also require 1/2 < p < 2. State both restrictions before using the formulas. A negative predicted quantity or reward is evidence that the proposed branch fails, not an admissible equilibrium. At the edges, a good or reward can be zero and uniqueness or full employment can change.

The production solution is globally optimal on this branch. For any feasible (X′,Y′), positive supporting rewards give pX′+Y′ = w(2X′+Y′)+r(X′+2Y′) ≤ wL+rK. The proposed fully employed bundle attains the bound. Because w,r > 0, equality requires both resources to bind; the two independent equations give a unique output bundle. Zero-profit competitive firms and factor owners can support it. This certificate proves the case without pretending that fixed coefficients provide a universal factor-proportions theorem.

At fixed goods prices, increasing L by ΔL while holding K fixed changes output by ΔX = 2ΔL/3, ΔY = −ΔL/3, as long as the new point stays in the cone. The labor-intensive good expands and releases capital by contracting the other industry; factor rewards do not change on this branch. At fixed endowments, increasing p gives dw/dp = 2/3 and dr/dp = −1/3. Both labor purchasing powers rise: d(w/p)/dp = 1/(3p²) > 0 and dw/dp > 0. Both capital purchasing powers fall: d(r/p)/dp = −2/(3p²) < 0 and dr/dp < 0. A relative goods-price change can thus create a real loss even after factors have moved between industries.

Worked example 2 — A national gain with a losing ownership group

Home owns (L,K) = (110,100), Foreign (100,110). Production is respectively (X,Y) = (40,30) and (30,40). In autarky, equal expenditure shares imply p = Y/X: Home p = 3/4, Foreign p = 4/3. Both prices lie in the positive-reward interval, so the diversification solutions are valid.

World output is (70,70). A common price p = 1, again inside the interval, gives each country income 70 and demand (35,35). Home exports 5 X for 5 Y; Foreign exports 5 Y for 5 X. Home is relatively labor abundant (110/100 > 100/110) and exports the labor-intensive good. National utility squared rises from 1,200 to 1,225 in each country.

Home factor rewards before and after trade
RewardAutarky p = 3/4Trade p = 1
w in Y per hour1/61/3
w/p in X per hour2/91/3
r in Y per machine service5/121/3
r/p in X per machine service5/91/3

A Home household owning only labor can buy more of either good per endowed hour. A household owning only capital services can buy less of either good. Its budget set strictly contracts despite the national opportunity to gain. With mixed ownership, evaluate wℓ + rk and the household's consumption prices; the industry label alone does not determine its welfare. Compensation requires an actual feasible transfer. Exercise 3 constructs one and checks both groups, rather than assuming that aggregate gains have already compensated them.

The two countries share factor rewards at their common trade prices here because both produce both goods with identical technologies, positive factor rewards and no wedges. Technology differences, specialization, heterogeneous factor quality, trade costs or taxes can break that conclusion. The signs just derived are a bounded illustration of the Heckscher–Ohlin and Stolper–Samuelson mechanisms, not an empirical claim about which factor loses in every trading country. Short-run sector-specific capital, unemployment and transition costs require other models.

The primary course route is MIT 14.54 Lecture 13 for factor prices and resource clearing. Our fixed-coefficient proof supplies its own global and boundary conditions.

MIT 14.54 Lecture 14 develops the trade and real-reward mechanisms under the two-factor framework.

Scale, market access and heterogeneous firms

A fixed resource cost F > 0 and constant marginal cost c give average cost F/q+c, decreasing with q > 0. Producing a larger quantity of the same variety can spread overhead. This internal economy of scale differs from an external economy in which an industry's size changes each firm's technology. Neither alone proves that every merger or trade reform raises welfare: pricing power, resource duplication, consumer valuation of variety and market-entry conditions matter.

To isolate export selection, consider existing domestic firms with known marginal costs ci > 0. Each can sell its own differentiated variety in one foreign destination. For this decision, other market conditions are held fixed and its residual inverse demand is P(q) = max{A−bq,0}, with A,b > 0. Prices and costs use a common transferable numeraire dollar. q is units delivered during the period; b is dollars per delivered-unit squared when quantity is measured as a period total. Delivering q requires production τq, where τ ≥ 1 is an iceberg requirement: τ−1 units are used up per delivered unit. The destination setup F > 0 is a real resource cost, avoidable before the decision, incurred only for positive exports. Domestic business and its already committed costs are unchanged.

πi(0) = 0;   πi(q) = [max{A−bq,0}−τci]q−F   for q > 0.

For q ≥ A/b, price is zero and profit is negative because costs are positive. These choices are dominated by staying out. On 0 < q < A/b, profit is (A−τci)q−bq²−F, strictly concave. If A ≤ τci, every positive q loses money. If A > τci, complete the square:

qi* = (A−τci)/(2b),   Vi = (A−τci)²/(4b),
πi(q) = Vi−F−b(q−qi*)².

Export q* if V > F, stay out if V < F, and allow both 0 and q* at equality. This comparison proves the global choice including the discontinuity at zero. For strictly positive c, an exporter can exist only if A > 2√(bF), and the cutoff is c ≤ [A−2√(bF)]/τ, with indifference at equality. If productivity is a = w/c at a fixed input wage w > 0, this is a minimum-productivity cutoff a ≥ τw/[A−2√(bF)]. The positive numerator condition cannot be omitted before squaring an inequality.

Worked example 3 — Lower trade costs change who exports

Let A = 50, b = 1, F = 64 and costs c = 12,20,28 for three otherwise identical firms. Initially τ = 3/2. Their delivered marginal costs are 18,30,42; positive-branch quantities are 16,10,4 and contributions V are 256,100,16. Subtracting setup gives 192,36,−48. The first two export; the third stays out with profit zero. The cost cutoff is (50−16)/(3/2) = 68/3, below 28.

Reduce τ to 1 while holding A,b,F,c fixed. Quantities become 19,15,11 and net export profits 297,161,57. The third firm now enters the destination. Delivered prices are 31,35,39 rather than the initial exporting firms' 34,40. This distinguishes the intensive margin (sales of existing exporters) from the extensive margin (which firms export). Shipping requirements and delivered sales are different quantities: initially the first exporter produces 24 units to deliver 16; after the change it produces 19 to deliver 19.

At given delivered demand, lower c or τ raises a firm's best achievable profit: every previously feasible q has weakly lower cost. The explicit formula gives the quantity response on the active branch. A reduction in b, a larger market at any given price with A fixed, also raises q* and V. It need not lower the optimal price, since P(q*) = (A+τc)/2 is independent of b. General-equilibrium entry or competitive pressure may also move A,b,w and domestic sales; those are not solved by holding residual demand fixed.

Selection is not the same as learning. Firms can have different export status with completely unchanged technologies. An exporter/nonexporter productivity gap is therefore not by itself evidence that exporting caused productivity growth. Nor does our destination decision prove that nonexporters shut their domestic plants or that an economy-wide productivity index rises. Those conclusions need domestic demand, entry, factor-market clearing, firm weights and an identified comparison. Trade can support differentiated two-way trade even without different national opportunity costs, but an allocation of varieties and its welfare requires a preference and entry model beyond this conditional decision.

See the actual method discussion in MIT 14.54 Lecture 17 for fixed costs, declining average cost and residual-demand profit choice.

Lecture 18's firm-heterogeneity section motivates the distinction between variable/fixed export costs and selection. We do not import its empirical estimates or claim to have solved its full industry reallocation mechanism.

A small-country tariff: transfers and resource losses

Switch to one competitive import market and a transferable numeraire. Domestic demand D(p) = max{120−2p,0} comes from marginal benefit MB(D) = 60−D/2 on 0 ≤ D ≤ 120; domestic supply S(p) = max{2p−20,0} comes from marginal cost MC(S) = 10+S/2. Thus gross benefit B(D) = 60D−D²/4 and cost C(S) = 10S+S²/4. Quasilinear preferences, an unbound numeraire budget and efficient allocation within each side make surplus an exact numeraire measure. Domestic producers and tariff revenue belong to domestic residents. There are no externalities, collection costs, retaliation or other wedges.

Foreign goods are perfectly substitutable. Initially a small importer can buy at a constant foreign price pf = 20. A specific tariff t ≥ 0 is dollars per imported unit, not a percentage of value. With positive imports, domestic price pd = 20+t; imports M = D−S = 60−4t. This branch requires t < 15. At t ≥ 15 no imports are profitable, domestic clearing gives pd = 35 and D = S = 50, and tariff revenue is zero. Do not extend negative imports or enforce equality pd = pf+t when trade has stopped. The no-import condition is pd ≤ pf+t.

CS = B(D)−pdD = (60−pd)²,
PS = pdS−C(S) = (pd−10)²,
R = tM,   WH = CS+PS+R = B(D)−C(S)−pfM.

The last equality follows by substituting M = D−S and pd−t = pf. It counts the foreign payment once and cancels domestic transfers. CS and PS formulas above apply on our positive-demand/positive-supply branches. R is not an additional resource produced by customs, and PS is not necessarily profit if an unchanged fixed cost must also be paid. Here none is present. Foreign receipts pfM can be balanced by exports of the numeraire; the domestic tariff payment is not a payment abroad.

Worked example 4 — Reconcile a tariff of five

Small-country one-period tariff ledger, numeraire dollars
ItemFree tradet = 5Change
Domestic price20255
D, S, M80,20,6070,30,40−10,10,−20
CS1,6001,225−375
PS100225125
Revenue0200200
National surplus WH1,7001,650−50

The consumer loss does not all disappear: 125 goes to domestic producers and 200 to government revenue. The remaining 50 is a resource loss. Production expands by ten units whose marginal domestic cost exceeds 20; the triangle is 5(10)/2 = 25. Consumption contracts by ten units whose marginal benefit exceeded the unchanged import cost; the other triangle is 25. Directly, B(70)−C(30)−20(40) = 2,975−525−800 = 1,650, agreeing with the transfer ledger.

For 0 ≤ t ≤ 15, the two triangles sum to 2t², so ΔWH = −2t². Beyond the prohibitive tariff the loss stays 450 rather than rising as that quadratic. Subject to this model's assumptions, t = 0 globally maximizes domestic surplus over every nonnegative tariff. A distributional objective, external cost or revenue-raising constraint would be a different problem; merely counting producer gains does not establish it.

Terms of trade: a foreign response changes national, not world, accounting

Replace constant foreign supply with a stated inverse export supply pf(M) = 10+M/6 for M ≥ 0. Model it as foreign competitive export producers with total opportunity cost CF(M) = 10M+M²/12, no separate foreign consumers of this good, and constant-price numeraire trade. Home is now large enough to affect its import price. Foreign firms take the market price, while their aggregate supply slopes upward. The government is assumed able to commit to t, with this response unchanged and no retaliation.

With positive trade, equate 140−4pd to M and use pd = 10+M/6+t. Solving gives

M = 60−(12/5)t,   pf = 20−(2/5)t,   pd = 20+(3/5)t,   0 ≤ t ≤ 25.

Import demand is strictly decreasing in pd and export supply is strictly increasing in pf; with their fixed tariff wedge the positive intersection is unique. The solution satisfies pd in [20,35] and pf in [10,20], keeping the domestic branches valid. At t ≥ 25, M = 0, pd = 35 and revenue is zero. At zero trade, 10 is the foreign marginal supply reservation price; no actual border transaction occurs. It is not meaningful to report an observed import terms of trade from a nonexistent transaction.

For an importing country exporting a numeraire priced at one, 1/pf improves as the import price falls. Let Δp = pd−20. Relative to free trade, the national decomposition is

ΔWH = (20−pf)M − ½Δp[(D0−D)+(S−S0)]
= 24t − (42/25)t²   for 0 ≤ t ≤ 25.

The first term reduces the payment on the imports still purchased: a terms-of-trade transfer from abroad. The two triangles measure domestic consumption and production distortions relative to the original price. This identity can be checked by substituting CS,PS,R; it does not treat foreign losses as a new world resource. Foreign producer surplus is pfM−CF(M) = M²/12. Therefore ΔWF = −24t+(12/25)t² and ΔWworld = −(6/5)t². At t ≥ 25, Home's change stays −450, Foreign's −300 and the world change −750.

Worked example 5 — The same tariff, a different incidence

At t = 5, pf = 18, pd = 23 and M = 48. Home consumes 74 and produces 26. CS = 37² = 1,369, PS = 13² = 169 and revenue = 5(48) = 240. National surplus is 1,778: ΔCS = −231, ΔPS = 69, ΔR = 240, hence ΔWH = 78. Foreign receives 18(48) = 864, distinct from the 240 collected domestically. The direct resource/payment calculation also gives B(74)−C(26)−864 = 3,071−429−864 = 1,778.

The terms-of-trade rectangle is (20−18)48 = 96. The two domestic triangles total ½(3)(6+6) = 18, leaving 78. Foreign producer surplus falls from 300 to 192, a loss of 108. World surplus falls by 30, despite Home's positive gain. Consumers at Home still lose even though the national unweighted sum rises.

On the positive-trade interval, dΔWH/dt = 24−(84/25)t and the second derivative is −84/25. Thus t* = 50/7 is the unique maximum there, with gain 600/7. At t = 0 the gain is zero; at and beyond 25 it is −450. These checks establish the global maximum over t ≥ 0. This is a conditional optimum against the fixed foreign response, not advice about an actual government's policy. Retaliation, demand changes, collection costs, international commitments or distributive weights require a new feasible set and objective.

The small/large-country distinction and surplus channels are developed in MIT 14.54 Lecture 20. Our inverse export supply, exact ledgers, corner thresholds and global optimum are synthetic derivations. No current law, tariff schedule or measured foreign response is asserted.

Reproduce choices and inspect the ledger

Download synthetic inputs, the standard-library benchmark and README. Keep the three files together and run python3 v06-c10-analysis.py. Exact rational strings preserve fractions such as 50/7; the output labels each tariff regime and preserves all optimal export quantities at indifference. The program covers the stated tariff schedules and conditional firm choices, not arbitrary trade equilibria.

Before reading a result, predict whether a tariff stops imports, whether foreign receipts differ from tariff revenue, and whether an export setup cost is avoidable. Change one valid parameter at a time. Explain why a lower iceberg requirement and a tariff reduction need not share the same resource accounting. A program that returns plausible quantities while omitting the government's revenue or the no-trade branch has not solved the stated welfare problem.

Exercises

  1. Keep Home's Ricardian technology and labor from Worked example 1, but give Foreign aC = aW = 1 and L = 120. Both countries retain √(CW) preferences. Compare absolute and comparative advantage. Test complete specialization with Home in cloth and Foreign in wheat, reject any inadmissible candidate, and solve the actual equilibrium including production, consumption, wages and balanced trade. Compare each country's utility with autarky.
  2. For the fixed-factor technology, at p = 1,K = 100, raise L from 110 to 113. Calculate output and factor rewards and explain the contraction of one sector. Then set L = 203. Explain why the diversification formulas fail; solve the global production problem, identify unused resources and give nonnegative factor prices supporting the solution. Do not use negative output.
  3. In Worked example 2, all Home labor belongs to one group and all Home capital services to another. Each group has √(XY) preferences, consumes its entire income and can receive a lump-sum transfer in Y units. Derive their autarky incomes and utilities. After trade, test a transfer of 15 from labor owners to capital owners. Does each group strictly gain relative to autarky? Derive the interval of transfers that makes both groups weakly better off. You may use e(p,u) = 2u√p, or derive it from the budget choice.
  4. In the export model let A = 50,b = 1,τ = 3/2,c = 68/3. Solve the entire export choice when F = 64, and when an avoidable F = 80. Then suppose the 80 has already been irreversibly paid regardless of current exports. Solve the current quantity and net profit, comparing shutdown. Finally explain why squaring a putative cutoff inequality without checking A−τc can give a wrong answer when A ≤ τc.
  5. For c = 20,A = 50,τ = 3/2,F = 64, reduce b from 1 to 1/2. Calculate delivered quantity, price, contribution, net profit and average export cost before and after. Does this larger residual market reduce the optimal price? Separately lower τ from 3/2 to 1 but reduce A from 50 to 30, keeping b = 1. Does the firm still export? Use the calculations to assess the claim that every trade-cost reduction expands every firm or proves learning from exporting.
  6. In the small-country tariff economy calculate prices, D,S,M,CS,PS,R and national welfare at t = 10 and t = 20. Give changes from free trade. If all tariff revenue is rebated to consumers, does the t = 10 welfare loss disappear? Explain why pd = 40 is not an equilibrium at t = 20.
  7. In the large-country economy derive the national-welfare change polynomial from CS,PS and revenue, without assuming the terms-of-trade formula. Prove the global maximizing nonnegative tariff, including no-trade tariffs. At that optimum give M,pf,pd, domestic gain, foreign loss and world loss. Identify two maintained assumptions whose failure invalidates this optimum.
  8. Replace the large-country tariff t = 5 with zero tariff and a real shipping requirement that uses five units of the numeraire good, worth five dollars, per delivered unit. Keep both supply/demand schedules and competitive delivery. Solve the prices and quantities. Reconcile domestic, foreign and world welfare relative to costless free trade and compare with Worked example 5. Can observations of the border price, domestic price and import quantity alone tell which wedge generated them? State the extra evidence required.
Complete solutions

  1. Foreign uses fewer hours in both goods, so it has absolute advantage in both. Opportunity costs are 1/2 at Home and 1 abroad; Home still has comparative advantage in cloth. Complete specialization would supply 60 cloth and 120 wheat. Equal expenditure shares would require p = 120/60 = 2, outside [1/2,1]. At p = 2 Foreign would prefer cloth, contradicting the proposed production.

    At p = 1 Home specializes in 60 cloth; Foreign is indifferent between sectors. World income is 60+120 = 180, giving world demand 90 of each good. Foreign therefore produces 30 cloth and 90 wheat, using 120 hours. Home consumes (30,30); Foreign (60,60). Home exports 30 cloth for 30 wheat, and Foreign reverses the trade. Home's wage is 1/2 wheat per hour; Foreign's is 1. Foreign's two sectors both cover that wage; Home wheat cannot. Home's utility squared rises from 450 to 900. Foreign's autarky consumption was already (60,60), so its utility is unchanged. Comparative advantage and feasible gains do not imply strictly positive gains for every country in every equilibrium.

  2. At L = 113, X = (226−100)/3 = 42 and Y = (200−113)/3 = 29. The extra three hours permit two extra X, while one less Y releases two machine services and one labor hour: the total net labor requirement is four minus one, or three. Both resources clear. Rewards stay w = r = 1/3 at the fixed goods price.

    At L = 203 the formulas give X = 102,Y = −1, violating nonnegativity. For any feasible bundle, X+Y ≤ X+2Y ≤ 100, so production value cannot exceed 100 at p = 1. X = 100,Y = 0 attains it, uses 200 labor and all 100 capital services, and leaves three labor hours unused. It is the unique maximizing bundle: attaining the bound requires Y = 0 and X = 100. Supporting rewards w = 0,r = 1 satisfy X unit cost 1 = p and Y unit cost 2 > 1. Excess labor has zero marginal value here; a negative wage from the invalid branch is unnecessary.

  3. Autarky p = 3/4, w = 1/6,r = 5/12. Group incomes are mL = 110/6 = 55/3 and mK = 100(5/12) = 125/3. The budget solution gives u = m/(2√p), so old utilities are 55/(3√3) and 125/(3√3). After trade, pretransfer incomes are 110/3 and 100/3. With transfer 15 they become 65/3 and 145/3, hence utilities 65/6 and 145/6 at p = 1. These exceed the old utilities: the squared differences are 575/108 and 575/108 respectively, both positive. Transfers conserve total income 70 and both groups can afford their chosen positive bundles.

    To protect capital owners, T ≥ 250/(3√3)−100/3. To protect labor owners, T ≤ 110/3−110/(3√3). Thus approximately 14.7792 ≤ T ≤ 15.4972; 15 is feasible and makes both strictly better off. The interval width is 70−40√3 > 0, since 70² > (40√3)². This is a feasible compensation construction under lump-sum implementation, not evidence that trade automatically implements the transfer.

  4. Delivered marginal cost is (3/2)(68/3) = 34; positive-branch q* = (50−34)/2 = 8, price 42 and contribution 64. At avoidable F = 64, both q = 0 and q = 8 maximize profit at zero; every other positive q does worse by (q−8)² on the positive-price branch, and zero-price output loses money. At avoidable F = 80, positive operation's best profit is −16, so staying out uniquely gives zero.

    If 80 is unavoidable, shutdown loses 80 and q = 8 loses only 16; choose 8. A sunk cost changes the comparison with shutdown, not the marginal condition. If A−τc ≤ 0, positive output has nonpositive gross margin and incurs F, so no export is profitable. Squaring would incorrectly convert a negative margin into a positive contribution expression; the interior positive-q candidate is not feasible on that branch.

  5. The delivered marginal cost is 30. Initially q = 10, price 40, contribution 100, net profit 36 and average export cost 30+64/10 = 182/5 = 36.4. At b = 1/2, q = 20, price remains 40, contribution 200, net profit 136 and average cost 30+64/20 = 166/5 = 33.2. More sales spread the same fixed resource cost; the optimal price formula (A+τc)/2 has not changed.

    With τ = 1,A = 30,b = 1, the positive-branch candidate is q = 5 at price 25, contribution 25 and net profit −39. The firm stays out. The beneficial direct cost change can be outweighed by a worsened residual demand curve. A claim about all firms therefore needs the other market responses. None of these calculations changes c, so they cannot establish productivity learning. Establishing such learning empirically requires an identified counterfactual accounting for selection and other demand/cost changes.

  6. At t = 10, pd = 30,D = 60,S = 40,M = 20. CS = 900,PS = 400,R = 200,WH = 1,500. Changes from free trade are −700,+300,+200 and −200. Rebating the 200 to consumers makes their combined consumption-surplus/rebate change −500; producers gain 300 and total loss stays 200. Revenue is counted once, whether retained or rebated under the stipulated dollar-for-dollar valuation.

    At t = 20 imports cease: pd = 35,D = S = 50,M = R = 0. CS = PS = 625 and WH = 1,250, a loss of 450; CS changes −975 and PS +525. A price of 40 would give D = 40,S = 60 and excess domestic supply. With no export outlet in this import-only market, it cannot clear. At 35, importing at delivered cost40 is unprofitable, consistent with zero imports.

  7. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 25, CS = (40−3t/5)² and PS = (10+3t/5)². Their combined change is −36t+18t²/25. Revenue is t(60−12t/5) = 60t−60t²/25. Adding gives ΔWH = 24t−42t²/25 = 600/7−(42/25)(t−50/7)². The unique maximizing tariff on this interval is 50/7. For t ≥ 25 the gain is the constant −450; thus no omitted no-trade tariff beats the interior maximum.

    At t* imports are 300/7, pf = 120/7 and pd = 170/7. Domestic gain is 600/7. Foreign surplus is (300/7)²/12 = 7,500/49 instead of 300, so its change is −7,200/49. World change is 4,200/49−7,200/49 = −3,000/49. The home gain is not a world gain. Retaliation changing foreign market access or the export-supply curve, a binding treaty constraint, real administration costs or a different distributive objective would each invalidate this exact optimum unless the problem were re-solved with them.

  8. Competitive delivery still implies pd = pf+5, so pf = 18,pd = 23,M = 48,D = 74,S = 26. But government revenue is zero: 5(48) = 240 units of the numeraire good, worth 240 dollars, are consumed in shipping. Home welfare is B(74)−C(26)−18(48)−5(48) = 1,538, or CS+PS = 1,369+169. Relative to free trade it changes −162, compared with the tariff's +78. The 240 difference is a real cost here, a domestic transfer in the tariff case.

    Foreign surplus remains 192, a change of −108. World welfare changes −270 = −162−108: the 30 loss from reduced trade plus shipping resources240. The same observed price wedge and quantities therefore do not identify a tariff transfer versus a real trade cost. Government receipt records, the legal/contractual instrument, delivery inputs and recipient/location evidence are needed. If a quoted freight charge includes profits or foreign service payments rather than pure resource consumption, its ownership and opportunity costs must be modeled before using this ledger.

Teach-back and Delayed check

Teach-back: explain to a skeptical worker how a country can gain from trade while a factor-owning group loses, why productive firms can be exporters without learning from exporting, and why tariff revenue is neither free wealth nor necessarily a resource loss. Give one equation and one assumption for each distinction.

Teach-back guide

A complete explanation links the feasible national budget P·QT ≥ P·QA to ownership income wℓ+rk: affordability of the old national bundle does not preserve every household budget. It states the factor model's diversification and technology assumptions. It then compares export contribution (A−τc)²/(4b) with avoidable F under A > τc; selection can occur with c unchanged, while a learning claim needs a counterfactual. Finally it reconciles CS+PS+tM = B−C−pfM, counting domestic revenue once and specifying ownership, numeraire valuation and any foreign response. Merely saying that trade is always good or always harmful does not explain these mechanisms.

Delayed check: without notes, compare a tariff t = 5 with t = 0 in both of the chapter's tariff economies. Recover the domestic and foreign prices, imports, national change and any foreign change. Then give the export decision for A = 40,b = 1,c = 16,τ = 1,F = 144, including all optimal quantities.

Delayed-check answer

Small country: foreign price20 unchanged, domestic price25, imports40 and national change−50; the foreign constant-price model does not supply a finite foreign producer-surplus schedule from which to calculate its total welfare change. Large country: foreign18,domestic23,imports48,national change78,foreign change−108,world change−30. For the firm, q* = (40−16)/2 = 12 and contribution144 equals the avoidable setup. Both zero and12 maximize profit at zero. A derivative alone identifies only the positive-output candidate and misses the stay-out optimum.

Evidence and the next question

These models distinguish technological opportunity cost, factor ownership, fixed-cost selection and market-power terms of trade. An empirical assessment needs technology and factor measurements, household ownership and prices, actual trade costs, fiscal recipients and a defensible counterfactual. Observing a wage change, an exporter premium or a tariff wedge does not select one causal mechanism by itself. Graduate trade work extends the theory to many goods, uncertain firm entry, general-equilibrium reallocation and policy games. Next, exchange rates and external balances separates goods trade from income, financing and valuation when international payments need not balance within a single goods period.

Sources and further study

  • Arnaud Costinot, MIT 14.54 — Lecture 8: Ricardian Trade Model (Fall 2016) — Primary instructor method route for unit-labor production, opportunity costs, specialization, incomplete-specialization boundaries and competitive wages. The chapter independently constructs and clears its two-country examples and proves the feasible-budget comparison.
  • Arnaud Costinot, MIT 14.54 — Lecture 13: Heckscher–Ohlin Model of Trade I (Fall 2016) — Primary instructor method route for factor mobility within a country, unit-cost equations, factor-market clearing and conditional factor-price equalization. The chapter's fixed-coefficient production and dual supporting-price proof are original specializations.
  • Arnaud Costinot, MIT 14.54 — Lecture 14: Heckscher–Ohlin Model of Trade II (Fall 2016) — Primary instructor method route for relative endowments, common technologies/preferences, specialization limits and the Stolper–Samuelson real-reward mechanism. The original chapter proves only its explicitly bounded fixed-coefficient case and computes actual ownership transfers.
  • Arnaud Costinot, MIT 14.54 — Lecture 17: Increasing Returns to Scale (Fall 2016) — Primary instructor method route for internal versus external scale economies, fixed costs, declining average cost, residual demand and the comparison of positive-operation profit with staying out.
  • Arnaud Costinot, MIT 14.54 — Lecture 18: Consequences of Increasing Returns, Theory and Evidence (Fall 2016) — Primary instructor method route for heterogeneous marginal costs, fixed/per-unit trade costs and exporter selection. Supports the motivation for separating intensive and extensive margins, not a causal learning estimate.
  • Arnaud Costinot, MIT 14.54 — Lecture 20: Trade Policy I, Tariffs (Fall 2016) — Primary instructor method route for specific tariffs, small versus large importers, import-demand/export-supply responses and the consumer/producer/revenue/terms-of-trade decomposition. The chapter independently derives its original schedules, direct resource ledgers and all tariff boundaries.
